claims.claim: The edit shifted the subject of the sentence to Godly ('June served Godly, but Godly still did not trust him.'), so the immediately following sentence 'He thought of killing Godly' now resolves 'He' to Godly, yielding the self-contradictory 'Godly thought of killing Godly.' In the source it is June, not Godly, who reflects on killing Godly. The edit fixed the distrust actor but left the pronoun antecedent pointing at the wrong actor.
claims.reason: Confirmed. Telling line 13 reads: 'June served Godly, but Godly still did not trust him. He thought of killing Godly, but then a pupil's son arrived...' The subject of the immediately preceding independent clause is Godly, so the default antecedent for 'He' is Godly, giving the incoherent 'Godly thought of killing Godly.' The source (corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt line 2219) clearly attributes the reflection to June: 'As the time passed in this manner, June reflected: "Dear me! Do what I will, he does not trust me. So shall I kill him with a knife in broad daylight? Or give him poison? Or butcher him like a beast?"' The source's structure is also contrastive-correct: 'he does not trust me' (June speaking, Godly = 'he') whereas the telling inverted who distrusts whom and then left the pronoun pointing at the wrong actor. The telling contradicts the source and is internally self-contradictory.

claims.claim: The telling's moral runs opposite to the source's lesson; source says sharing your home with a stranger destroyed Creep (the guest is the host's ruin), while the telling prescribes the reverse remedy (be a mindful, boundary-respecting host), and the body does not support the telling's moral either since Creep sets the boundary and still dies.
claims.reason: Source moral at corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt:3868 reads 'With no stranger share your house; Leap, the flea, killed Creep, the louse' — the lesson is that admitting the stranger (guest Leap) is what killed the host Creep. The source frame (line 3904) explicitly names hospitality as her undoing: 'she agreed, since courtesy was her hobby.' The telling (corpus/age/9+/PT015-leap-and-creep.txt:15) inverts this: 'Being a good host means being mindful of your guests' needs and respecting their boundaries, lest you suffer the consequences' — prescribing the opposite remedy. The telling's body also fails to support that moral: Creep scolds Leap (line 5) and lays down the boundary/condition (line 9), yet still dies (line 11), so boundary-respecting hosting is not shown to avert the disaster. The source clearly contradicts the telling's moral.

claims.claim: Line 11 casts the fable's thief as the spared party: "One counselor, Hook-Nose, suggested that the thief should not be killed." The source's spared party is the owl court's suppliant guest (the crow Live-Strong), not the fable's thief.
claims.reason: Confirmed against corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt. In the frame story, Foe-Crusher the owl king is deciding the fate of his suppliant guest Live-Strong the crow. Flame-Eye tells the fable 'The Old Man with the Young Wife' and then applies it (line 10767): 'Thus advantage may be anticipated from a benefactor, thief though he be. How much more from a suppliant guest? ... he should not be killed.' Hook-Nose replies at line 10769: 'O King, he should not be killed' — the 'he' is the suppliant guest, not the thief. The fable's thief merely replies and leaves (lines 10757-10765); he is never threatened or discussed as a candidate for killing. So the telling's line 11 'Hook-Nose, suggested that the thief should not be killed' misassigns the spared party, exactly as the flag states.

claims.claim: The telling's appended moral (line 15: "True worth is not measured by appearance or family background, but by one's actions and character") inverts the source's lesson. The source chapter's authority closes the fable on noble lineage being decisive: the king refuses the potter despite his virtues and recites the stanza ending "But in your family, my boy, / No elephants are slain." The telling's moral asserts the opposite about family background, and it contradicts the telling's own body line (line 13: the king refused because "he had no noble blood"). The source's narrator-tag in complete.txt (12270-12278) puts the lesson on a trickster ruined by telling the truth ("lets the truth slip out, like Fight-Firm... is sure to lose his victory"), which the telling's moral also drops.
